title: Troubleshooting
text:
Troubleshooting the HAR Distributed Framework is easier when failures are isolated according to the processing layer in which they occur.
Because the system combines networking, ROS communication, BLE acquisition, local inference, synchronization, central fusion, logging, and visualization, checking components in the correct order avoids debugging downstream modules when the actual problem originates earlier in the pipeline.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Recommended Diagnostic Order
The recommended troubleshooting sequence is shown in Figure 1.






Figure 1: Recommended diagnostic sequence for isolating runtime failures in the distributed HAR framework.



The general rule is:

Verify the lowest common dependency first and move downstream only after that component is confirmed to be working.

For example, do not troubleshoot central fusion until the local prediction streams have been verified.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Edge Node Cannot Reach the Central Node
text:
Edge Node Cannot Reach the Central Node
First verify basic IP communication:
ping <CENTRAL_IP>
If the central node cannot be reached, troubleshoot the local network before inspecting ROS.
Check the device address:
hostname -I
or:
ip addr
Detailed network configuration is documented in Network & Time Synchronization.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
ROS Master Is Not Reachable
Verify:
echo $ROS_MASTER_URI
echo $ROS_IP
On an edge device, ROS_MASTER_URI should reference the central node.
Then test:
rostopic list
If this command cannot communicate with the ROS master, verify:

the central roscore process;
IP connectivity;
environment variables;
firewall configuration; and
Docker networking if ROS runs inside a container.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Custom Probs Message Is Not Available
text:
Custom Probs Message Is Not Available
Check:
rosmsg show har_msgs/Probs
If ROS cannot locate the message, source the Catkin workspace containing har_msgs:
source <CATKIN_WS>/devel/setup.bash
Then repeat:
rosmsg show har_msgs/Probs

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Sensor Is Not Detected
Inspect nearby Bluetooth devices:
bluetoothctl
Then:
scan on
Verify that the expected MetaMotionRL device appears.
If necessary, restart Bluetooth:
sudo systemctl restart bluetooth
Then retry sensor discovery.
Physical sensor assignment and BLE preparation are documented in Wearable Sensor Setup.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Wrong Sensor Connects to an Edge Node
text:
Wrong Sensor Connects to an Edge Node
Verify the MAC address configured for that edge process.
Each edge role should maintain a fixed relationship among. The required sensor-to-model assignment consistency is illustrated in Figure 2.






Figure 2: Relationship among body location, wearable sensor, MAC address, edge node, and local model.



A BLE connection can be technically successful while still being incorrect if the process connects to the wearable assigned to another body location.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Sensor Connects but No Data Are Produced
text:
Sensor Connects but No Data Are Produced
Check the edge-node terminal for acquisition errors.
Then verify that the expected sensor modality is being configured.
For example, a quaternion branch and an accelerometer–gyroscope branch do not use the same acquisition pipeline.
If the physical connection is valid but model input never becomes available, inspect the acquisition and buffering stages described under Edge Nodes.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Local ROS Node Does Not Appear
text:
Local ROS Node Does Not Appear
Check:
rosnode list
The expected edge roles are:
/chest_node
/left_hand_node
/right_hand_node
/left_knee_node
/right_knee_node
If the corresponding node is missing, inspect the Python process running on that Jetson.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Local Topic Is Missing
Check:
rostopic list
The expected prediction topics are:
/har/probs/chest
/har/probs/left_hand
/har/probs/right_hand
/har/probs/left_knee
/har/probs/right_knee
If only one topic is missing, troubleshoot the corresponding edge node rather than the complete distributed system.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Topic Exists but No Messages Are Published
text:
Topic Exists but No Messages Are Published
Inspect the topic:
rostopic echo /har/probs/<sensor>
Check its rate:
rostopic hz /har/probs/<sensor>
Then verify that the inference pipeline has received the start signal:
rostopic echo /har/start
A running Python process does not necessarily mean that inference is currently enabled.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Local Model Does Not Load
Verify that: MODEL_PATH
points to the correct trained parameter file.
Also verify the corresponding scaler file.
The following must match:
Sensor modality
Window dimensions
Channel ordering
Scaler
Model architecture
Trained parameters
Model compatibility is documented under Models & Data.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Model Loads but Local Predictions Are Incorrect
text:
Model Loads but Local Predictions Are Incorrect
Check the sensor-to-model assignment first.
A model can load successfully while receiving data from the wrong body location or in the wrong channel order.
Also verify:
sensor_id
K
probs
using:
rostopic echo /har/probs/<sensor>

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Central Node Does Not Appear
Check:
rosnode list
The central HAR process should appear as:
/central_har_node
If it does not, inspect the terminal running:
central_node_ros_main.py

title: Troubleshooting
section: All Five Local Topics Exist but No Global Prediction Appears
text:
All Five Local Topics Exist but No Global Prediction Appears
First verify that the framework is enabled:
rostopic echo /har/start
Then inspect:
rostopic echo /har/probs/global
If the five local streams are active but the global stream is absent, inspect the central-node terminal for:

Model-Loading Messages
Probability-Vector Size Errors
Synchronization Messages
Failover Events
Timestamp-Related Problems

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Central Model File Is Missing
The current central implementation expects:
nn_central_fold1.pth
through its configured MODEL_PATH.
A particularly important behavior of the current implementation is that if this file is not found, the central node can continue after issuing a warning and instantiate the model with random weights.
Therefore, a running /har/probs/global topic does not by itself prove that the correct trained fusion model is being used.
Always inspect the startup output and confirm that the expected model was successfully loaded.






Warning



Do not collect experimental data if the central process reports that the trained model file was not found.
The system may continue generating numerically valid probability vectors using untrained parameters.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Probability Vector Sizes Are Inconsistent
The central node expects all local predictions participating in fusion to contain the same value of: K
For the current implementation: K = 6
Check each topic:
rostopic echo /har/probs/<sensor>
and confirm that every local message contains six probabilities.

title: Troubleshooting
section: ATS Does Not Produce Synchronized Groups
text:
ATS Does Not Produce Synchronized Groups
Verify that all five streams are active:
rostopic hz /har/probs/chest
rostopic hz /har/probs/left_hand
rostopic hz /har/probs/right_hand
rostopic hz /har/probs/left_knee
rostopic hz /har/probs/right_knee
Then verify clock synchronization:
chronyc tracking
and:
chronyc sources -v
The current implementation uses:
SYNC_SLOP_SEC = 0.05
QUEUE_SIZE    = 10
corresponding to a maximum ATS tolerance of approximately:
50 ms
Detailed behavior is documented in Communication & Synchronization.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Central Node Switches to ZOH
A transition such as:
FAILOVER -> ZOH
indicates that ATS has not generated valid synchronized callbacks within the configured failover conditions.
Check whether one or more local streams have:

Stopped
Slowed significantly
Lost network connectivity
Become temporally misaligned
Stopped publishing current timestamps

The fallback itself is expected behavior when normal synchronized operation cannot be maintained.

title: Troubleshooting
section: System Remains in ZOH After a Node Recovers
text:
System Remains in ZOH After a Node Recovers
Verify that all five local streams have resumed normal publication.
Then confirm that synchronized ATS events are occurring continuously.
The central implementation requires ATS to remain stable for the configured recovery interval before switching back to normal synchronized operation.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Determine the Current Fusion Mode
Inspect:
rostopic echo /har/probs/global
The central implementation identifies the source mode in the global message through sensor_id.
Depending on the active mode, the value can identify synchronized or fallback operation.
This is useful when diagnosing whether a global prediction originated from normal ATS fusion or ZOH fallback.

title: Troubleshooting
section: ROS Topics Exist but ATS Behavior Is Unstable
text:
ROS Topics Exist but ATS Behavior Is Unstable
A network connection alone is not sufficient for timestamp-based synchronization.
Check Chrony on every distributed device.
On an edge node:
chronyc tracking
and:
chronyc sources -v
Large clock offsets can cause predictions representing similar movement intervals to appear temporally incompatible at the central node.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Chrony Does Not See the Central Time Source
text:
Chrony Does Not See the Central Time Source
Verify:

Central-Node IP Connectivity
The server <CENTRAL_IP> iburst entry on the edge node
The allow <LOCAL_SUBNET> configuration on the central node
That the Chrony service is running

Check:
sudo systemctl status chrony
Configuration details are documented in Network & Time Synchronization.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
No Run Directory Is Created
Verify that:
experiment_manager_node.py
is running.
Then verify:
rostopic echo /har/start
The manager creates a new run when it receives the experiment start signal.
The default output location is:
~/har_runs/

title: Troubleshooting
section: Run Directory Exists but inference.csv Is Empty
text:
Run Directory Exists but inference.csv Is Empty
Verify that the manager receives:
/har/probs/global
using:
rostopic echo /har/probs/global
If the global stream itself is empty, troubleshoot the central node first.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
latency.csv Contains Empty Timing Fields
Inspect the global message:
rostopic echo /har/probs/global
Verify that timing fields such as:
t0_ns
t_last_local_send_ns
t_send_ns
contain valid values.
The experiment manager cannot calculate a latency component when its required timestamps are unavailable.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
power.csv Is Empty
Verify:
jtop
If the command is unavailable, confirm that jetson-stats is installed.
Power logging is optional and does not prevent prediction or latency logging from operating.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Cannot Calculate Classification Accuracy
The current experiment_manager_node.py records:
pred_label
but does not independently generate:
true_label
Ground truth must therefore be supplied or associated during the experimental workflow before classification metrics can be calculated.
See Experiments & Logs.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Global Prediction Exists but Unity Does Not Update
text:
Global Prediction Exists but Unity Does Not Update
First confirm:
rostopic echo /har/probs/global
If the global output exists, the inference system itself is functioning.
The visualization data path is illustrated in Figure 3.






Figure 3: Data flow from the central HAR prediction to the Unity visualization interface.



Verify:
rostopic echo /har/probs/global_ui
If /har/probs/global exists but /har/probs/global_ui does not, inspect the relay or visualization bridge rather than the central fusion model.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Unity Start Button Does Not Start the Experiment
text:
Unity Start Button Does Not Start the Experiment
Verify the external control topic:
rostopic echo /har/start_ui
Then verify that the corresponding system-level signal reaches:
/har/start
If /har/start_ui changes but /har/start does not, inspect the start-control relay.
If /har/start becomes true but inference still does not begin, return to the edge and central runtime sections.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Probabilities Are Produced but Predictions Are Clearly Incorrect
text:
Probabilities Are Produced but Predictions Are Clearly Incorrect
A technically functioning pipeline can still be semantically incorrect.
Check:



Item
Required Consistency




Sensor assignment
Correct body location


Modality
Quaternion or ACC + GYRO as expected


Channel order
Same as training


Window size
Same as model training


Scaler
Corresponding model/scaler pair


Local model
Correct node-specific parameters


Class order
Identical across all classifiers


Sensor order
Same order used to train central fusion


Central model
Correct trained parameter file



This category of failure is especially important because ROS topics may appear completely normal.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Central Input Order Is Wrong
The central fusion model depends on a fixed semantic ordering of local probability vectors.
The implementation uses:
Chest
Left Knee
Right Hand
Left Hand
Right Knee
when constructing the central fusion input.
Changing this ordering without retraining the fusion model can produce incorrect classifications even though the input still contains the expected 30 numerical values.

title: Experiments & Logs
text:
The HAR Distributed Framework includes an experiment-management layer that records the information required to inspect predictions, timing behavior, and central-node power consumption during real-time execution.
The current runtime implementation uses:
to organize each experiment into an independent run directory.

title: Experiments & Logs
text:
Experiment Logging Pipeline
The relationship between the distributed runtime and the generated experiment files is illustrated in Figure 1.






Figure 1: Experiment logging pipeline used by the distributed HAR framework.



The experiment manager observes:

The global prediction stream;
The five local prediction streams;
The experiment start/stop signal; and
Power information available from the central Jetson.

Logging operates independently from the inference models and does not modify the local or central prediction process.

title: Experiments & Logs
text:
Run Organization
By default, experiment data are stored under:
~/har_runs/
Each new run creates a timestamp-based directory using the format:
YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS_run
For example:
~/har_runs/
└── 2026-08-30_14-32-15_run/ 
    ├── inference.csv
    ├── latency.csv
    ├── power.csv
    └── summary.json
A new directory is created when the experiment manager receives:
/har/start = true
The active files are closed and summarized when:
/har/start = false

title: Experiments & Logs
text:
inference.csv
The inference.csv file records the global prediction stream received by the experiment manager.
The current implementation stores:







Column
Description




run_id
Identifier assigned to the experiment


t_session_sec
Time elapsed since the beginning of the run


t_rx_epoch_sec
Epoch time at which the global prediction is received


sensor_id
Identifier included in the global prediction message


seq
Global prediction sequence number


K
Number of activity classes


pred_label
Predicted class obtained using argmax


pred_conf
Probability associated with the predicted class


dropped_pct
Degradation/drop indicator propagated by the central node


probs
Complete global probability vector



The predicted class is obtained as:
pred_label = argmax(probs)
For the current six-class HAR configuration:
probs = [p0, p1, p2, p3, p4, p5]
The activity-class mapping is documented under Models & Data.






Important



The current experiment_manager_node.py does not write a true_label field to inference.csv.
Therefore, classification accuracy cannot be computed from this file alone unless ground-truth labels are provided by another component or merged during post-processing.

title: Experiments & Logs
text:
latency.csv
The latency.csv file contains timing information used to decompose the real-time response of the distributed system.
The main fields are:







Column
Description




run_id
Experiment identifier


t_session_sec
Time elapsed since experiment start


t_rx_ns
Time at which the global message reaches the experiment manager


t0_ns
Reference time associated with the distributed input


t_last_local_send_ns
Latest local publication time contributing to the global prediction


t_send_ns_global
Time at which the central prediction is transmitted


L_local_ms
Distributed local-processing interval


L_central_ms
Central-processing interval


L_net_global_ms
Global-message transmission interval


L1_e2e_ms
End-to-end latency


L_local_chest_ms
Latest measured chest-node local latency


L_local_left_knee_ms
Latest measured left-knee local latency


L_local_right_hand_ms
Latest measured right-hand local latency


L_local_left_hand_ms
Latest measured left-hand local latency


L_local_right_knee_ms
Latest measured right-knee local latency


L_local_mean_ms
Mean of the available local-node latencies


L_local_max_ms
Maximum of the available local-node latencies

title: Experiments & Logs
text:
Latency Decomposition
The experiment manager derives the principal latency components directly from the timestamps carried by the distributed prediction messages.

Local Processing
L_local_ms =
(t_last_local_send_ns - t0_ns) / 1e6


Central Processing
L_central_ms =
(t_send_ns_global - t_last_local_send_ns) / 1e6


Final Network Transfer
L_net_global_ms =
(t_rx_ns - t_send_ns_global) / 1e6


End-to-End Latency
L1_e2e_ms =
(t_rx_ns - t0_ns) / 1e6
These components make it possible to distinguish the time associated with distributed local processing, central processing, and delivery of the final global prediction.






Note



L_local_ms represents the interval up to the latest local prediction participating in the central output.
The file also records the latest independently measured local latency for each sensing node, together with their mean and maximum values.

title: Experiments & Logs
text:
power.csv
When power monitoring is enabled, the experiment manager uses jtop from the jetson-stats package to sample power information from the central Jetson.
The current implementation records:



Column
Description




run_id
Experiment identifier


t_session_sec
Time elapsed since experiment start


t_epoch_sec
Epoch timestamp of the power measurement


power_tot_w
Total power measurement


power_tot_avg_w
Average total power reported by jtop


power_sys5v_w
SYS5V power measurement when available


raw_power_dict
Complete power dictionary returned by jtop



The default sampling configuration is:
10 Hz
The available power rails depend on the Jetson platform.






Warning



Power-rail names are hardware-dependent.
Fields such as SYS5V, VDD_IN, or POM_5V_IN should not be assumed to exist on every Jetson model.


If jtop is unavailable, the prediction and latency logs can still operate while power monitoring remains disabled.

title: Experiments & Logs
text:
summary.json
When a run finishes, the experiment manager creates:
summary.json
The current summary includes:
run_id
start_time_ros_sec
rows_inference
rows_latency
rows_power
power_backend
notes
This file provides a compact description of the completed experiment and the number of samples written to the main logs.

title: Experiments & Logs
text:
Optional Local Edge Logs
The local edge implementations can also record sensor-level information independently from the central experiment manager.
The confirmed edge scripts include optional CSV logging containing:

raw sensor windows;
scaled model-input windows;
local prediction probabilities;
sequence information; and
local timing information.

A typical filename follows a structure similar to:
<sensor_id>_run<id>_<timestamp>_raw_window_probs.csv
These files are primarily useful when debugging or validating the processing performed by an individual edge node.
They are separate from the centralized experiment directory created by experiment_manager_node.py.

title: Experiments & Logs
text:
Synchronization Metrics
Synchronization quality is evaluated using the temporal dispersion among the local predictions included in the same fusion event.
The primary metric is:
sync_span_ms
Conceptually:
sync_span_ms =
latest local timestamp
-
earliest local timestamp
This value measures how temporally close the five local probability messages are when they are grouped for central fusion.
The synchronization mechanism itself is documented in Communication & Synchronization.

title: Experiments & Logs
text:
Synchronization Analysis
The project also includes a synchronization-analysis script that processes:
central_sync_metrics.csv
The primary required field is:
sync_span_ms
When available, the analysis also considers:
fusion_mode
window_ref_span_ms
local_send_span_ms
The synchronization analysis calculates statistics including:
Number of samples
Mean
Standard deviation
Minimum
Median
P90
P95
P99
Maximum
and can generate a distribution of the synchronization span.






Note



sync_span_ms is the primary synchronization metric.
window_ref_span_ms and local_send_span_ms are complementary diagnostic measurements and should not be interpreted as substitutes for the actual ATS acceptance criterion.

title: Experiments & Logs
text:
Experiment Verification
After stopping a run, verify that the expected directory was created:
ls ~/har_runs/
Inspect the most recent run:
ls ~/har_runs/<RUN_ID>/
The expected files are:
inference.csv
latency.csv
power.csv
summary.json
Inspect the first rows of a log using:
head ~/har_runs/<RUN_ID>/inference.csv
or:
head ~/har_runs/<RUN_ID>/latency.csv
Verify that rows were recorded throughout the experiment.

title: Experiments & Logs
text:
Quick Data Inspection
The number of recorded global predictions can be inspected using:
wc -l ~/har_runs/<RUN_ID>/inference.csv
Similarly:
wc -l ~/har_runs/<RUN_ID>/latency.csv
Remember that the first row contains the CSV header.

title: Experiments & Logs
text:
Post-Experiment Analysis
The generated logs support several categories of system-level analysis.



Analysis
Primary Data

End-to-end latency

Latency decomposition
latency.csv

latency.csv

Classification metrics additionally require ground-truth activity labels.
These labels must be associated with the recorded prediction sequence before computing metrics such as:
Accuracy
Precision

title: Models & Data
text:
The HAR Distributed Framework uses sensor-specific neural networks at the edge and a prediction-level fusion model at the central node.
This section defines the data representations, activity classes, input windows, local HAR models, and central fusion model used by the framework.

title: Models & Data
text:
Activity Classes
The framework recognizes six activities.



Class ID
Activity




0
Sitting


1
Folding Clothes


2
Sweeping


3
Walking


4
Moving Boxes


5
Riding a Bike



All local classifiers and the central fusion model therefore produce six output probabilities.
A prediction vector has the form:
[p0, p1, p2, p3, p4, p5]
where each element represents the confidence associated with one activity class.

title: Models & Data
text:
Sensor Representations
The local HAR models operate on two types of sensor representations.

Accelerometer and Gyroscope
Nodes configured for inertial motion data use:
ax, ay, az, gx, gy, gz
where:

ax, ay, and az represent tri-axial acceleration; and
gx, gy, and gz represent tri-axial angular velocity.

The resulting input contains:
6 channels


Quaternion Orientation
Nodes configured for orientation information use:
w, x, y, z
The resulting input contains:
4 channels






Important



The input modality must match the model deployed on the corresponding edge node.
A model trained with quaternion inputs cannot be used directly with an accelerometer–gyroscope input, and vice versa.

title: Models & Data
text:
Sampling and Windowing
The real-time framework operates at a nominal sampling rate of:
50 Hz
Sensor measurements are grouped into windows containing:
50 samples
which corresponds to approximately:
1 second
of sensor data.
Therefore, depending on the sensor representation, a local model receives one of the following input structures:



Representation
Window
Channels
Input Size




Quaternion
50 samples
4
50 × 4


Accelerometer + Gyroscope
50 samples
6
50 × 6



The real-time inference pipeline processes complete 50-sample windows before generating a new local prediction.

title: Models & Data
text:
Offline and Real-Time Windowing
The dataset preparation and real-time deployment use the same fundamental window length but differ in how windows are generated.

Offline Processing
During offline dataset preparation, windows use:
Window size: 50 samples
Stride:      25 samples
This introduces overlap between consecutive samples used for model development and evaluation.


Real-Time Processing
During real-time execution, each edge node accumulates incoming measurements until a complete 50-sample window is available for inference.
The resulting window is then converted into the tensor representation expected by the corresponding local model.

title: Models & Data
text:
Local HAR Models
Each edge node executes a sensor-specific CNN-LSTM classifier.
The relationship between one sensor window and the local prediction is illustrated in Figure 1.






Figure 1: Input and output organization of a local CNN-LSTM classifier.



The local CNN-LSTM architecture combines:

Convolutional processing for feature extraction from the sensor sequence
Recurrent processing for temporal modeling

Each local classifier contains:
9,990 trainable parameters
and produces:
6 output probabilities
regardless of whether the input representation contains four or six channels.

Prediction-Level Fusion
The central node combines the outputs generated by the five local classifiers.
Each edge model provides:
6 probabilities
With five edge nodes, the fusion input therefore contains:

The complete fusion process is illustrated in Figure 2.

  Left Knee probabilities,
  Right Knee probabilities
]
forming a 30-element input vector.

title: Models & Data
text:
Central Fusion Model
The central classifier is implemented as a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP).
Its role is not to process raw inertial measurements.
Instead, it learns how to combine the class-confidence information generated independently by the five local CNN-LSTM classifiers.
The fusion model contains:
2,374 trainable parameters
and generates the final six-class probability distribution used by the framework. The complete distributed model hierarchy is illustrated in Figure 3.






Figure 3: Distributed HAR model hierarchy from local CNN-LSTM classifiers to the global prediction.

text:

The distributed architecture performs feature extraction and local classification close to the wearable sensors.
Consequently, the central node receives compact prediction vectors instead of continuously receiving full raw sensor windows.

title: Central Node
text:
The central node performs the system-level processing of the HAR Distributed Framework.
It receives the local predictions generated by the five edge nodes, coordinates them temporally, executes the central fusion model, and produces the final global Human Activity Recognition prediction.
The central node also supports experiment logging and communication with the visualization interface.

title: Central Node
text:
Central Processing Pipeline
The main processing stages executed by the central node are summarized in Figure 1.






Figure 1: Processing pipeline executed by the central node of the HAR Distributed Framework.



The central pipeline consists of four main stages:

Prediction Reception
Temporal Synchronization
Central Fusion
Global Prediction Generation

Logging and visualization operate as downstream consumers of the system output.

title: Central Node
text:
Prediction Reception
Each edge node publishes the probability distribution generated by its local HAR model.
The central node receives predictions from the five sensing locations:

Chest
Left Hand
Right Hand
Left Knee
Right Knee

The received messages contain the information required by the central processing pipeline, including the local probability vector and associated metadata.
The exact ROS topics, message structure, timestamps, and sequence fields are documented under Communication & Synchronization.

title: Central Node
text:
Temporal Coordination
Predictions are generated independently by the distributed edge nodes.
As a result, the central node must coordinate the incoming messages before they are provided to the fusion model.
This stage ensures that the local predictions used together correspond as closely as possible to the same time interval.
The central implementation also includes mechanisms for maintaining operation when one or more predictions are temporarily delayed or unavailable.
Detailed synchronization behavior is documented under Communication & Synchronization.

title: Central Node
text:
Central Fusion
Once a compatible set of local predictions is available, the central node combines them and provides the resulting input to the fusion model.
The fusion model receives information from all five local classifiers and produces a system-level probability distribution over the supported activities.
The central node therefore performs a different role from the edge devices:



Processing Level
Function




Edge Nodes
Sensor-level inference


Central Node
Prediction-level fusion



The detailed fusion-model architecture, input organization, and trained model files are documented under Models & Data.

title: Central Node
text:
Global Prediction
The fusion model generates a probability distribution representing the final HAR output.
The system selects the resulting global activity prediction from this distribution.
The global output can then be consumed by:

Experiment Logging
Performance Measurement Tools
The Real-Time Visualization Interface

The execution workflow is documented later under Running the Framework.

title: Central Node
text:
Experiment Logging
The central node records information required to evaluate the real-time behavior of the distributed system.
Depending on the experiment, the recorded information includes:

Local Prediction Information
Global Predictions
Synchronization Measurements
Communication Timing
Central Processing Timing
End-To-End System Timing

The exact log files, fields, and analysis workflow are documented under Experiments & Logs.

title: Central Node
text:
Visualization Output
The global prediction is also made available to the visualization layer.
In the implemented system, this output can be consumed by the Unity-based graphical interface used to display the recognized activity during real-time execution.
The visualization procedure is documented as part of Running the Framework.

Responsibility

Confirm that:

The ROS environment is available
The central node can receive local prediction messages
Predictions from all five edge nodes are visible
Synchronization is operating correctly
The fusion model loads successfully
A valid global probability vector is generated

Tip



Verify prediction reception before troubleshooting the fusion model.
If one or more edge streams are missing, the problem may originate in the distributed communication layer rather than the central inference component.

title: Central Node
text:
Troubleshooting

One or More Edge Predictions Are Missing
Verify the corresponding edge node first.
Confirm that:

Local inference is running;
A valid probability vector is being generated; and
The local prediction is being published.

Then verify the communication configuration under Communication & Synchronization.


Fusion Model Does Not Load
Verify that:

The expected model file is available
The configured model path is correct
PyTorch can load the model
The model definition matches the saved parameters
The runtime environment is compatible

Detailed model information is documented under Models & Data.


Local Predictions Arrive but No Global Prediction Is Generated
Check whether the central synchronization stage is producing a valid set of inputs for fusion.
If the incoming predictions are available but cannot be combined, continue with Communication & Synchronization.


Logging Is Not Generated
Verify that:

The logging component is enabled
The output directory exists
Sufficient storage is available
The process has permission to write to the configured location

Log organization is documented under Experiments & Logs.

Sensor acquisition must therefore provide data at a rate compatible with the input expected by the framework.

title: Software Environment
text:
This section describes the software environment required to execute the HAR Distributed Framework on the NVIDIA Jetson devices.
The objective is to ensure that each computing node provides the runtime components needed for sensor acquisition, neural network inference, ROS communication, and distributed system execution.
For hardware preparation, see the Getting Started section.

title: Software Environment
text:
Software Stack
The framework relies on the following main software components:



Component
Purpose




NVIDIA Jetson Linux environment
Base operating environment


Docker
Containerized execution


ROS Noetic
Distributed communication middleware


Python 3
Framework implementation


PyTorch
Neural network inference


CUDA
GPU acceleration where supported


Chrony
Clock synchronization between devices



Chrony configuration is documented separately under Network & Time Synchronization.

title: Software Environment
text:
Host and Container Environment
The runtime environment is organized into the software layers shown in Figure 1.






Figure 1: Software stack used by the HAR Distributed Framework.



The Jetson host provides the NVIDIA operating environment and access to the hardware resources.
Docker containers provide the runtime environment used by the HAR framework and help maintain a consistent software configuration across the distributed devices.

title: Software Environment
text:
Jetson Host Environment
Before configuring the framework, verify that the Jetson operating system is working correctly.
Basic system information can be checked with:
cat /etc/os-release
Check the NVIDIA L4T release using:
cat /etc/nv_tegra_release
The Jetson model can be identified using:
cat /proc/device-tree/model
These commands are useful when documenting or troubleshooting differences between Jetson platforms.

title: Software Environment
text:
Docker
Docker is used to execute the framework components in isolated runtime environments.
Verify that Docker is installed:
docker --version
You can also verify that the Docker service is running:
sudo systemctl status docker
A successful installation should return the installed Docker version and show the Docker service as active.






Note



The HAR implementation uses Docker containers containing the ROS and Python runtime required by the distributed nodes.
Container creation and framework execution are documented later under Framework and Running the Framework.

title: Software Environment
text:
ROS Noetic
The distributed communication infrastructure is based on ROS Noetic.
ROS provides communication between the edge devices and the central node using a distributed publish/subscribe architecture.
If ROS is available in the current runtime environment, verify the ROS distribution using:
rosversion -d
The expected distribution for the implemented framework is:
noetic
If ROS is executed inside a Docker container, this command should be executed from within the corresponding container.






Tip



ROS network configuration such as ROS_MASTER_URI, ROS_IP, host addresses, and communication verification is documented under Network & Time Synchronization and Communication & Synchronization.

title: Software Environment
text:
Python Environment
The framework implementation uses Python 3 for tasks including:

Sensor acquisition
Local inference
ROS publishers and subscribers
Central fusion
Experiment logging
Supporting utilities

Verify the installed Python version using:
python3 --version
The corresponding Python environment must contain the packages required by the framework components executed on that device.

title: Software Environment
text:
PyTorch
PyTorch is used to load and execute the trained HAR models.
Verify that PyTorch is available using:
python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__)"
To verify whether CUDA is accessible from PyTorch:
python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())"
If CUDA is available, additional information can be checked with:
python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.version.cuda)"
and:
python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'CUDA not available')"






Note



The exact PyTorch and CUDA versions may vary between Jetson platforms.
A centralized GPU evaluation used a PyTorch environment based on:
PyTorch 2.0.0+nv23.05
CUDA 11.4
These versions should not be assumed to apply automatically to every edge device.

title: Flashing Jetson Boards
text: This section describes a general procedure for installing an NVIDIA Jetson Linux environment from the command line.

title: Flashing Jetson Boards
text:
When Is Flashing Required?
Use this procedure when:

The Jetson does not have an operating system
A clean NVIDIA Jetson environment is required
The current installation needs to be replaced or recovered
The device must be prepared before performing additional system configuration

If the Jetson already boots correctly and provides the required software environment, continue with the next setup stage.

title: Flashing Jetson Boards
text:
Requirements
The documented command-line flashing workflow requires:

An NVIDIA Jetson or compatible reComputer device
A separate Linux host computer
A compatible NVIDIA Jetson Linux / L4T release
The corresponding L4T Driver Package (BSP)
The corresponding Sample Root Filesystem
A USB connection between the host computer and the Jetson device

The original workflow used an Ubuntu 18.04 Linux host for the flashing process.






Warning



The Jetson Linux / L4T release must be compatible with the specific Jetson module and carrier board being flashed.
Always verify platform support before downloading and flashing an image.

title: Flashing Jetson Boards
section: 1. Download the NVIDIA Jetson Linux Files
text:
1. Download the NVIDIA Jetson Linux Files
On the Linux host computer, open the NVIDIA Jetson Linux archive:
NVIDIA Jetson Linux Archive
Select a release compatible with the target Jetson platform.
Download both:

L4T Driver Package (BSP)
Sample Root Filesystem

The downloaded files typically follow names similar to:
Jetson_Linux_Rxx.x.x_aarch64.tbz2
Tegra_Linux_Sample-Root-Filesystem_Rxx.x.x_aarch64.tbz2

title: Flashing Jetson Boards
text:
2. Prepare the Flashing Directory
Create a working directory on the Linux host:
mkdir -p ~/jetson_flash
cd ~/jetson_flash
Copy the downloaded BSP and Sample Root Filesystem files into this directory.
The expected structure is approximately:
jetson_flash/
├── Jetson_Linux_Rxx.x.x_aarch64.tbz2
└── Tegra_Linux_Sample-Root-Filesystem_Rxx.x.x_aarch64.tbz2

title: Flashing Jetson Boards
section: 3. Extract the BSP and Assemble the Root Filesystem
text:
3. Extract the BSP and Assemble the Root Filesystem
Extract the NVIDIA Jetson Linux package:
tar xf Jetson_Linux_Rxx.x.x_aarch64.tbz2
Then extract the Sample Root Filesystem into the Jetson root filesystem:
cd Linux_for_Tegra/rootfs/

sudo tar xpf ../../Tegra_Linux_Sample-Root-Filesystem_Rxx.x.x_aarch64.tbz2
Return to the Linux_for_Tegra directory:
cd ..
Apply the NVIDIA binaries:
sudo ./apply_binaries.sh
A successful execution should complete the preparation of the root filesystem before flashing.

title: Flashing Jetson Boards
section: 4. Put the Jetson in Recovery Mode
text:
4. Put the Jetson in Recovery Mode
Before flashing, place the target Jetson device in Force Recovery Mode and connect it to the Linux host computer through USB.
The exact recovery procedure depends on the Jetson module and carrier board.
Refer to the corresponding hardware documentation for the target device before continuing.






Tip



Verify that the host computer detects the Jetson in recovery mode before executing the flashing command.

title: Flashing Jetson Boards
text:
5. Flash the Jetson
From the Linux_for_Tegra directory, the general flashing command follows:
sudo ./flash.sh <BOARD_CONFIG> mmcblk0p1
where:
<BOARD_CONFIG>
must correspond to the target Jetson module and carrier board.
For example, a board-specific configuration may result in a command of the form:
sudo ./flash.sh jetson-nano-emmc mmcblk0p1






Warning



Do not copy the example board configuration without verifying that it matches the Jetson platform being flashed.
The board configuration passed to flash.sh is hardware-specific.


The flashing process may take several minutes.

title: Flashing Jetson Boards
text:
6. First Boot
After the flashing process completes:

Disconnect the recovery-mode jumper or restore the board to its normal boot configuration
Disconnect the flashing USB connection if appropriate
Power-cycle or restart the Jetson
Complete the initial operating system setup

Once the device boots successfully, verify that the installed NVIDIA environment is available before continuing with the HAR framework configuration.

title: Flashing Jetson Boards
text:
Verification
After the first boot, basic system information can be checked with:
cat /etc/os-release
and:
cat /etc/nv_tegra_release
The Jetson should boot normally and report the expected operating system and NVIDIA L4T release.
If these checks succeed, continue with the remaining system preparation steps.

title: Flashing Jetson Boards
text:
Troubleshooting

QEMU Binary Not Available
If the flashing process reports an error similar to:
QEMU binary is not available, looking for QEMU from host system
install the required package on the Linux host:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install qemu-user-static


Flashing Does Not Start
Verify that:

The Jetson is in Force Recovery Mode
The USB connection is working
The selected L4T release supports the target Jetson
Both NVIDIA packages were extracted correctly
The correct board configuration is being passed to flash.sh

title: Flashing Jetson Boards
text:
Recommendations

Use a native Linux host for the flashing process
Avoid virtual machines when possible
Verify Jetson module and carrier-board compatibility before selecting an L4T release
Do not reflash devices that already contain a compatible and working system unless there is a specific reason to do so

title: Flashing Jetson Boards
text:
References
Additional platform-specific information is available from:

NVIDIA Jetson Linux Archive
Seeed Studio Wiki

text:

If additional storage is required, continue with:
Storage Expansion →
If the Jetson already provides sufficient storage, continue directly with Software Environment.

git clone https://github.com/WearNET/HAR-Distributed-Framework.git

title: Getting Started
text:
Recommended Setup Order
If the system is being reproduced from unconfigured hardware, prepare the environment in the following order: Steps 1 and 2 are optional; that is, if you need to flash your Jetson and expand the device’s storage, you must do so. Otherwise, if you already have a Jetson running Ubuntu 20.04, you don’t need to do this again.

1. Prepare the Jetson Boards
Install the appropriate NVIDIA Jetson operating environment.
Flash Jetson Boards →


2. Configure Storage
Prepare additional storage when required by the Jetson platform.
Storage Expansion →


3. Configure the Software Environment
Install and configure the runtime components required by the framework.
This includes the container environment, communication middleware, Python environment, and machine learning dependencies.
Software Environment →.


4. Configure Network and Time Synchronization
Connect the distributed devices to the local network and configure a common time reference between nodes.
Network & Time Synchronization →


5. Configure the Wearable Sensors
Prepare the wearable sensing devices and verify communication with their corresponding edge nodes.
Wearable Sensor Setup →


6. Deploy the Framework
Configure the software components responsible for:

Edge Inference

title: System Overview
text:
The HAR Distributed Framework is a multi-node wearable computing architecture developed for real-time Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using distributed embedded processing.
Instead of continuously transmitting raw sensor measurements to a single computing device, the framework performs local inference close to the sensing source. Each edge node generates activity probabilities that are transmitted to a central node, where the distributed predictions are synchronized and fused to obtain the final system-level activity prediction.

title: System Overview
text:
System Architecture
The framework is organized into four main layers:

Wearable sensing
Edge inference
Communication and synchronization
Central prediction fusion

The relationship among these layers is illustrated below.





The distributed configuration uses five wearable sensing locations:

Chest
Left Hand
Right Hand
Left Knee
Right Knee

Each wearable sensing stream is associated with an embedded edge computing node responsible for local processing and inference.
A separate central computing node coordinates the system-level decision process.

title: System Overview
text:
Edge and Central Processing
The framework separates computation into two levels.

Edge Processing
Each edge node processes data from its associated wearable sensor and executes a local HAR model.
The output of the local model is an activity probability vector:
[p0, p1, p2, p3, p4, p5]
These probabilities represent the local model confidence for the supported activity classes.
Rather than transmitting the complete raw sensor stream to the central node, the edge devices communicate these local predictions.


Central Processing
The central node receives predictions generated independently by the distributed edge nodes.
Before performing global inference, the incoming predictions are temporally coordinated so that information generated by different sensing locations can be combined consistently.
The synchronized local probability vectors are then provided to the central fusion model, which generates the final global activity prediction.

title: System Overview
text:
System Data Flow
The information flow through the complete framework is summarized below.





At a high level, the processing sequence is:

Wearable sensors acquire motion and orientation information.
Edge devices process their corresponding sensor streams.
Local HAR models generate activity probabilities.
Local predictions are transmitted through the distributed network.
The central node synchronizes the incoming predictions.
The fusion model combines the synchronized information.
A global HAR prediction is generated.
The result can be recorded and forwarded to the visualization interface.

Detailed sensor configuration, model inputs, and inference parameters are documented separately under Models & Data and Framework Implementation.

title: System Overview
text:
Communication and Synchronization
Communication between the edge nodes and the central node is performed at the prediction level.
This means that the distributed network primarily exchanges model outputs rather than continuously transmitting complete raw sensor windows for centralized inference.
The communication principle is illustrated below.





The implementation uses distributed communication mechanisms to exchange predictions together with the timing information required for system coordination.
Because the local predictions originate from independent computing devices, synchronization is required before central fusion.
The framework therefore includes mechanisms for:

Aligning predictions according to their timestamps;
Handling small differences in prediction arrival times; and
Maintaining system operation when a local prediction is temporarily unavailable.

The detailed ROS communication structure, message format, timestamps, synchronization strategy, and fallback mechanisms are documented in Communication & Synchronization.

title: System Overview
text:
Central Prediction Fusion
After synchronization, the probability vectors generated by the five local classifiers are provided to the central fusion model.





The fusion stage combines information from the different wearable sensing locations and produces a single probability distribution representing the global HAR prediction.
The architecture, input organization, training, and deployment of the local and central models are documented in Models & Data.

title: System Overview
text:
System Outputs
The global prediction generated by the framework is used by two main components.

Experiment Logging
The system records information required for subsequent performance analysis, including predictions and timing-related measurements.
The complete logging structure and experimental workflow are documented in Experiments & Logs.


Visualization
The global HAR output can also be forwarded to a graphical interface for real-time visualization of the recognized activity and system predictions.
The visualization component is documented as part of the framework execution workflow.

title: Storage Expansion
text: This section describes how to expand the available storage of a compatible Jetson-based system using an NVMe SSD connected through an M.2 M-Key slot.

title: Storage Expansion
text:
When Is Storage Expansion Useful?
Storage expansion is useful when the onboard storage is not sufficient for:

The operating system
Docker images and containers
Python and machine learning dependencies
Trained models
Experiment logs
Additional development resources

The procedure documented here moves the system root filesystem to an NVMe SSD while preserving the original root filesystem stored in the Jetson’s internal storage.

title: Storage Expansion
text:
Requirements
The procedure requires:

A Jetson-based system with an M.2 M-Key slot
An NVMe SSD
An existing working Jetson operating system
Sufficient access privileges to modify the storage configuration

The procedure was originally performed on a reComputer platform using an NVMe SSD.






Important



The Jetson must already boot correctly before performing this procedure.
Storage expansion does not replace the operating system flashing procedure.

title: Storage Expansion
text:
1. Install the NVMe SSD
Power off the Jetson device and install the NVMe SSD in the available M.2 M-Key slot.
Refer to the corresponding carrier-board hardware instructions for the exact installation procedure.
The device used for the original procedure is shown below.




Example reComputer platform used for NVMe storage expansion.



After installing the SSD, power on the Jetson and verify that the device is detected by the operating system.

title: Storage Expansion
text:
2. Prepare the SSD
Open the Ubuntu Disks utility.
The SSD should appear in the list of available storage devices.





Select the SSD and choose Format Disk.





Use a GPT partition table.





Create a new partition using the available storage space.





Continue with the partition creation process.





Format the partition using the Ext4 filesystem.





Once completed, the SSD is ready to receive a copy of the Jetson root filesystem.

title: Storage Expansion
text:
3. Download the Root-on-NVMe Utility
Open a terminal and clone the rootOnNVMe repository:
git clone https://github.com/limengdu/rootOnNVMe.git
cd rootOnNVMe/
This utility provides the scripts used to copy the existing root filesystem and configure the system to use the NVMe SSD.

title: Storage Expansion
text:
4. Copy the Root Filesystem
Execute:
./copy-rootfs-ssd.sh
The script copies the existing root filesystem from the Jetson internal storage to the SSD.
The execution time depends on the amount of data currently stored in the root filesystem.

title: Storage Expansion
text:
5. Configure Boot from NVMe
After the copy operation completes, execute:
./setup-service.sh
This configures the service required to use the SSD as the system root filesystem.





Restart the Jetson after the configuration is complete.

title: Storage Expansion
text:
Verification
After rebooting, verify that the system is using the NVMe SSD as the root filesystem.
A useful command is:
df -h /
You can also inspect available block devices using:
lsblk
The root filesystem should correspond to the NVMe storage device.
The original implementation showed the expanded storage after reboot as illustrated below.

title: Storage Expansion
text:
NVMe Device Path
The rootOnNVMe scripts assume the SSD partition is located at:
/dev/nvme0n1p1
Before running the scripts, verify the actual device path using:
sudo fdisk -l
or:
lsblk






Warning



If the SSD partition does not correspond to /dev/nvme0n1p1, the device path used by the rootOnNVMe scripts must be updated before continuing.
The original procedure identifies the following files as containing the default path:
copy-rootfs-ssd.sh
data/setssdroot.service
data/setssdroot.sh

title: Storage Expansion
text:
Recovery Behavior
The expansion procedure does not remove the original root filesystem stored in the internal eMMC.
This provides a useful recovery mechanism.
If the SSD is removed, the system can still boot from the original internal storage, assuming the original installation remains intact.

title: Storage Expansion
text:
Troubleshooting

SSD Is Not Detected
Verify that:

The SSD is correctly installed
The carrier board supports the installed NVMe device
The SSD is visible using lsblk or sudo fdisk -l
The M.2 slot supports NVMe storage



System Does Not Boot from the SSD
Check:

That the root filesystem copy completed successfully
That setup-service.sh executed without errors
That the correct NVMe partition path is configured
That the SSD contains a valid Ext4 filesystem



Incorrect NVMe Device Path
Use:
lsblk
to determine the actual SSD partition.
Update the rootOnNVMe configuration if the partition differs from:
/dev/nvme0n1p1

title: Storage Expansion
text:
Next Step
Once the Jetson hardware and storage are ready, continue with:
Software Environment
If no storage expansion was required, this page can be skipped entirely.

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
The HAR Distributed Framework operates across multiple independent computing devices. Before deploying the HAR software, all Jetson nodes must be able to communicate through the local network and share a common time reference.
This section covers the basic network and clock configuration required by the distributed system.

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
Network Roles
The distributed deployment uses one central node and multiple edge nodes connected to the same local network.
The central node provides two important services:

The ROS master used by the distributed ROS environment
The reference clock used to synchronize the edge devices.

The edge nodes connect to the central node through the local network.






Note



The specific IP addresses depend on the deployment.
Throughout this documentation, placeholders such as <CENTRAL_IP> and <EDGE_IP> are used when an address is installation-specific.

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
Verify Network Connectivity
Before configuring ROS or Chrony, verify that every device is connected to the same local network.
Check the IP addresses of a Jetson using:
hostname -I
or:
ip addr
From each edge node, verify connectivity to the central device:
ping <CENTRAL_IP>
Similarly, the central node should be able to reach each edge device:
ping <EDGE_IP>
The distributed configuration should not continue until bidirectional network connectivity is available.

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
ROS Multi-Machine Configuration
ROS Noetic uses a master process to coordinate communication between nodes.
In the implemented framework, the distributed devices use the central Jetson as the ROS master.

Central Node
On the central node, configure:
export ROS_MASTER_URI=http://<CENTRAL_IP>:11311
export ROS_IP=<CENTRAL_IP>
The ROS master can then be started using:
roscore


Edge Nodes
Each edge node must point to the same ROS master:
export ROS_MASTER_URI=http://<CENTRAL_IP>:11311
export ROS_IP=<EDGE_IP>
For example, each edge device uses its own address for ROS_IP while keeping the central address in ROS_MASTER_URI.
The general configuration is therefore:



Device
ROS_MASTER_URI
ROS_IP




Central Node
Central IP
Central IP


Chest Node
Central IP
Chest Node IP


Left Hand Node
Central IP
Left Hand Node IP


Right Hand Node
Central IP
Right Hand Node IP


Left Knee Node
Central IP
Left Knee Node IP


Right Knee Node
Central IP
Right Knee Node IP









Important



ROS_IP must identify the device on which the ROS process is running.
Do not assign the central node IP as ROS_IP on the edge devices.

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
Container Network Configuration
The HAR framework executes its ROS components inside Docker containers.
The ROS networking variables must therefore also be available inside the corresponding container.
The required environment variables are:
ROS_MASTER_URI
ROS_IP
The central and edge containers must preserve the same network relationships described above.
Detailed container startup commands are documented later under Running the Framework.

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
Verify ROS Communication
After starting roscore on the central device, verify the ROS environment from an edge node.
Check the master address:
echo $ROS_MASTER_URI
Check the local ROS address:
echo $ROS_IP
Then test access to the distributed ROS environment:
rostopic list
If the edge device can retrieve the topic list from the central ROS master, basic ROS connectivity is working.






Tip



Network connectivity using ping does not guarantee that ROS is configured correctly.
Always verify ROS communication independently after confirming IP connectivity.

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
Why Clock Synchronization Is Required
The distributed nodes generate predictions independently.
Because timestamps originate from different physical devices, their system clocks must be aligned before timing information can be compared reliably.
Clock synchronization is required for:

Prediction timestamp comparison
Distributed message alignment
Communication latency analysis
Synchronization measurements
End-to-end timing evaluation

The framework uses Chrony to maintain a common time reference across the distributed devices.

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
Chrony Architecture
The central Jetson acts as the local time reference for the distributed system.
Each edge node synchronizes its system clock against the central Jetson using Chrony, ensuring that timestamps generated on different devices can be compared consistently during synchronization and latency analysis.
The role of Chrony in the distributed architecture is illustrated in Figure 1.






Figure 1: Chrony synchronization architecture used by the distributed HAR framework.

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
Install Chrony
Install Chrony on the required devices using:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install chrony
The main configuration file is:
/etc/chrony/chrony.conf

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
Configure the Central Node
The central node must allow the edge devices on the local network to use it as a time source.
A deployment-specific Chrony configuration may include:
allow <LOCAL_SUBNET>
local stratum 10
For example, <LOCAL_SUBNET> should correspond to the subnet used by the distributed Jetson network.






Warning



Do not copy a subnet value from another deployment.
Use the subnet assigned to the local network hosting the HAR system.


Restart Chrony after modifying the configuration:
sudo systemctl restart chrony

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
Configure the Edge Nodes
Each edge node should use the central Jetson as its time source.
In /etc/chrony/chrony.conf, configure the central node address as:
server <CENTRAL_IP> iburst
Restart Chrony:
sudo systemctl restart chrony
Repeat this configuration on every edge device.

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
Verify Clock Synchronization
Check the current synchronization status using:
chronyc tracking
Inspect the available time sources using:
chronyc sources -v
The central Jetson should appear as the synchronization source on each edge device.
A healthy Chrony configuration should indicate that the device is synchronized and that the central node is being used as the active time source.

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
Recommended Verification Order
Verify the distributed infrastructure in this order:

Confirm that every device has a valid local IP address.
Verify bidirectional connectivity using ping.
Confirm ROS_MASTER_URI and ROS_IP.
Start the ROS master on the central node.
Verify ROS access from each edge node.
Verify Chrony connectivity.
Confirm clock synchronization using chronyc tracking.
Confirm the active time source using chronyc sources -v.

Only after network communication and clock synchronization are working should the distributed HAR components be started.

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
Troubleshooting

Edge Node Cannot Reach the ROS Master
Verify:
ping <CENTRAL_IP>
and:
echo $ROS_MASTER_URI
echo $ROS_IP
Confirm that roscore is running on the central node.


ROS Works Locally but Not Across Devices
Check that:

The devices are on the same reachable network
ROS_MASTER_URI points to the central node
ROS_IP corresponds to the current device
The relevant ports are not blocked
The Docker network configuration allows communication with the host network



Chrony Does Not Synchronize
Check:
chronyc sources -v
and:
chronyc tracking
Verify that:

The central node is reachable;
The edge node uses the correct central IP;
The central Chrony configuration allows clients from the local subnet; and
The Chrony service is running.

Check the service using:
sudo systemctl status chrony

title: Network & Time Synchronization
text:
Next Step
Once network communication and clock synchronization are working correctly, continue with:
Wearable Sensor Setup
This prepares the MetaMotionRL devices and verifies communication between each wearable sensor and its corresponding edge computing node.

title: Edge Nodes
text:
The edge nodes execute the sensor-level processing required by the HAR Distributed Framework.
Each edge device is associated with one wearable sensing location and runs the software required to acquire sensor data, prepare the model input, perform local inference, and transmit the resulting prediction to the central node.
The five edge nodes follow the same general software pipeline.

title: Edge Nodes
text:
Edge Node Software Pipeline
The processing stages executed locally before communicating with the central node are shown in Figure 1.






Figure 1: Software pipeline executed by each edge computing node.



The local pipeline consists of six main stages:

Sensor Acquisition
Sample Buffering
Input Preparation
Local Model Inference
Prediction Generation
ROS Publication

The sensing configuration and model inputs associated with each node are documented separately under Models & Data.

title: Edge Nodes
text:
Sensor Acquisition
Each edge node receives measurements from its assigned MetaMotionRL sensor through Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE).
The acquisition component is responsible for:

Establishing communication with the assigned wearable sensor
Receiving the required sensor stream
Maintaining continuous data acquisition
Forwarding incoming samples to the local processing buffer

Wearable sensor pairing, physical placement, and BLE verification are covered in Wearable Sensor Setup.

title: Edge Nodes
text:
Sample Buffer
Incoming measurements are accumulated locally until enough data are available to construct an input for the HAR model.
The buffer isolates continuous sensor acquisition from neural network inference and allows the edge node to prepare model inputs from incoming measurements.
Detailed window size, sampling rate, and signal organization are documented under Models & Data.

title: Edge Nodes
text:
Input Preparation
Before inference, the buffered sensor data are converted into the input representation expected by the local model.
This stage may include operations such as:

Selecting the required sensor channels
Organizing measurements in the expected order
Constructing the model input tensor
Applying any preprocessing required by the trained model

The exact input configuration is node-dependent and is therefore documented with the corresponding model definitions under Models & Data.

title: Edge Nodes
text:
Local Inference
Once the model input is available, the edge node executes its trained local HAR model.
Each local model processes information from one wearable sensing location and produces a probability distribution over the supported activity classes.
Conceptually, the output has the form:
[p0, p1, p2, p3, p4, p5]
The edge node does not make the final system-level activity decision.
Instead, the probability vector becomes the local contribution that will later be synchronized and combined by the central node.
The architecture and training of the local models are documented under Models & Data.

title: Edge Nodes
text:
Prediction Output
After inference, the local probability vector is prepared for transmission to the central node.
The outgoing information includes the prediction together with the metadata required by the distributed framework, such as identification and timing information.
The exact ROS message structure, sequence information, timestamps, and topic organization are documented under Communication & Synchronization.

title: Edge Nodes
text:
Timing Information
The edge implementation records timing information associated with local processing.
These measurements are used later to characterize the contribution of the edge devices to the overall real-time performance of the distributed system.
Timing measurement fields and the resulting experiment logs are documented under Experiments & Logs.

title: Edge Nodes
text:
Common Edge Node Structure
The five edge nodes use the same general processing pattern:



Edge Node
Local Responsibility




Chest
Sensor acquisition and local HAR inference


Left Hand
Sensor acquisition and local HAR inference


Right Hand
Sensor acquisition and local HAR inference


Left Knee
Sensor acquisition and local HAR inference


Right Knee
Sensor acquisition and local HAR inference



What changes between nodes is primarily the assigned sensor, input configuration, and trained local model.
Those node-specific differences are documented under Models & Data.

title: Edge Nodes
text:
Interaction with the Central Node
The edge nodes operate independently until a local prediction is generated.
Once available, each prediction is transmitted through ROS to the central computing node.
The central node is then responsible for:

Receiving predictions from all edge devices
Coordinating them temporally
Handling temporarily unavailable inputs
Performing central fusion
Generating the global HAR prediction

These operations are described in Central Node and Communication & Synchronization.

title: Edge Nodes
text:
Verification
An edge node should be verified incrementally before the complete distributed system is started.
Confirm that:

The assigned wearable sensor is detected
Sensor measurements are being received
The local buffer is being updated
The trained model loads correctly
Local inference executes without errors
A valid probability vector is generated
Prediction messages can be published
Local timing information is available when logging is enabled







Tip



Validate one edge node completely before deploying all five simultaneously.
This makes it easier to separate sensor, model, ROS, and network problems during initial setup.

title: Edge Nodes
text:
Troubleshooting

Sensor Data Are Not Available
Return to Wearable Sensor Setup and verify the BLE connection, sensor identity, and sensor-to-node assignment.


Local Model Does Not Load
Verify that:

The correct model file is available
The configured model path is correct
The Python/PyTorch environment is compatible
The model corresponds to the input configuration assigned to that node

Model organization is documented under Models & Data.


Inference Runs but No Prediction Is Received Centrally
First verify that local inference is producing a valid output.
If the local prediction exists but is not reaching the central node, continue troubleshooting under Communication & Synchronization.


ROS Communication Is Not Available
Verify the base ROS network configuration described in Network & Time Synchronization.

text:
Related Documentation
Use the following sections for details intentionally excluded from this page:

Models & Data — Signal configuration, input windows, local model architecture, and trained model files.
Communication & Synchronization — ROS topics, message format, timestamps, and distributed synchronization.
Running the Framework — Commands used to start the edge nodes during normal operation.

title: Edge Nodes
text:
Next Step
Continue with:
Central Node
The next section describes the software responsible for receiving distributed predictions, coordinating them, executing the fusion model, and producing the global HAR output.

title: Communication & Synchronization
text:
The HAR Distributed Framework uses ROS Noetic to exchange local activity predictions between the five edge nodes and the central node.
Communication occurs at the prediction level: each edge node publishes the probability vector generated by its local HAR model together with metadata required for identification, timing, and synchronization.
Before continuing, the distributed network and device clocks should already be configured as described in Network & Time Synchronization.

title: Communication & Synchronization
text:
Communication Architecture
Each edge node publishes its local prediction through a dedicated ROS topic.
The central node subscribes to all five prediction streams and coordinates the incoming messages before central fusion.
The distributed prediction topics are:



Edge Node
ROS Topic




Chest
/har/probs/chest


Left Hand
/har/probs/left_hand


Right Hand
/har/probs/right_hand


Left Knee
/har/probs/left_knee


Right Knee
/har/probs/right_knee



The central node generates the global prediction through:
/har/probs/global
A visualization-oriented output is also available through:
/har/probs/global_ui

title: Communication & Synchronization
text:
Prediction Message
Local predictions are exchanged using the custom ROS message:
har_msgs/Probs
The message contains both classification results and metadata required by the distributed runtime.
The implemented message structure includes:



std_msgs/Header
header


string
sensor_id


uint32
seq


uint64
t0_ns


uint64
t_send_ns


uint8
K


float32[]
probs


float32
dropped_pct




Message Fields



Field
Purpose




header
ROS message header and timestamp


sensor_id
Identifies the originating sensing node


seq
Local prediction sequence number


t0_ns
Initial timestamp associated with the prediction pipeline


t_send_ns
Time at which the local prediction is transmitted


K
Number of activity classes


probs[]
Activity probability vector


dropped_pct
Packet/data-drop information when applicable



The probability vector contains the local model output:
[p0, p1, p2, p3, p4, p5]
The interpretation of the six classes is documented under Models & Data.

title: Communication & Synchronization
text:
Local Publication
After completing local inference, each edge node:

Generates the activity probability vector
Assigns the corresponding sensor identifier
Updates the sequence number
Records timing information
Packages the information into har_msgs/Probs
Publishes the message to its node-specific ROS topic

The central node therefore receives five independent prediction streams.

title: Communication & Synchronization
text:
Central Reception
The central node subscribes to:
/har/probs/chest
/har/probs/left_hand
/har/probs/right_hand
/har/probs/left_knee
/har/probs/right_knee
Because these messages are produced on physically independent devices, they do not necessarily arrive at exactly the same time.
The synchronization layer determines which predictions can be combined before the central fusion model is executed.

title: Communication & Synchronization
text:
Approximate Time Synchronization
Under normal operating conditions, the central node uses ROS:
ApproximateTimeSynchronizer
to group predictions that are sufficiently close in time.
The implemented configuration uses:
Synchronization tolerance (slop): 0.05 s
Queue size: 10
Therefore, messages whose timestamps fall within approximately:
50 ms
can be considered part of the same synchronized prediction set.






Note



Approximate synchronization does not require the five predictions to have identical timestamps.
Instead, it allows a controlled temporal tolerance between independently generated messages.


When compatible predictions from all required nodes are available, the synchronized set is forwarded to the central fusion process.

title: Communication & Synchronization
text:
Synchronization Span
For each synchronized prediction set, the framework can measure the temporal difference between the earliest and latest participating prediction.
Conceptually:
sync_span = latest_timestamp - earliest_timestamp
This measurement provides an indication of how closely aligned the distributed predictions are before fusion.
The resulting synchronization metrics are documented under Experiments & Logs.

title: Communication & Synchronization
Communication & Synchronization
text:
Zero-Order Hold Fallback
When a current prediction from one node is temporarily unavailable, the system can reuse the most recent valid prediction from that node.
This strategy follows a Zero-Order Hold (ZOH) approach.
The decision process used by the ZOH fallback mechanism is illustrated in Figure 1.






Figure 1: Zero-Order Hold fallback behavior when a current edge-node prediction is unavailable.



The fallback allows the central fusion process to continue operating during short communication interruptions.






Important



ZOH does not generate a new prediction.
It temporarily reuses the last valid probability vector received from the affected node.

title: Communication & Synchronization
text:
Watchdog Mechanism
A watchdog mechanism monitors the availability of the distributed prediction streams. Its role is to determine whether each edge node is actively providing sufficiently recent predictions.
When all nodes are operating normally, the central system uses approximate synchronized prediction sets. If one or more nodes become unavailable, the framework can transition to the fallback mechanism.
When valid communication is restored, the system returns to normal synchronized operation. The transition between normal synchronized operation and the fallback mechanism is illustrated in Figure 2.






Figure 2: Synchronization, watchdog, ZOH fallback, and recovery behavior of the central node.

title: Communication & Synchronization
text:
Central Fusion Trigger
Central fusion is executed once a valid set of local probability vectors is available.
This set may originate from:

A normally synchronized ATS event; or
The fallback mechanism when temporary prediction loss occurs.

The resulting input contains one probability vector from each sensing location.
The fusion model itself is documented under Models & Data.

title: Communication & Synchronization
text:
Global Prediction Output
After central fusion, the system publishes the resulting global prediction.
The primary output topic is:
/har/probs/global
A visualization-specific output is also provided through:
/har/probs/global_ui
These outputs can be consumed by logging tools, visualization components, or other applications connected to the HAR framework.

title: Communication & Synchronization
text:
Start and Stop Control
The real-time framework also includes ROS-based execution control.
The visualization layer can publish:
/har/start_ui
which is used to control the system-level start signal:
/har/start
The complete operational procedure is documented under Running the Framework.

title: Communication & Synchronization
text:
Verification
Before running a full experiment, verify the communication layer incrementally.

Verify Edge Topics
From the ROS environment, check:
rostopic list
The expected local prediction topics should be visible.


Inspect a Local Prediction
For example:
rostopic echo /har/probs/chest
Verify that:

sensor_id is correct;
sequence numbers are increasing;
timestamps are being generated;
K has the expected value; and
probs contains the expected number of elements.



Check Publication Rate
For example:
rostopic hz /har/probs/chest
Repeat the test for the remaining edge nodes.


Verify Global Output
Once the five distributed inputs are available:
rostopic echo /har/probs/global
A valid global prediction indicates that reception, synchronization, and fusion are operating together.

title: Communication & Synchronization
text:
Troubleshooting

One Edge Topic Is Missing
Verify the corresponding edge node under Edge Nodes.
Confirm that local inference is running and that prediction messages are being published.


Topic Exists but Messages Do Not Arrive
Verify the base ROS network configuration described in Network & Time Synchronization.


Synchronization Does Not Trigger
Check that:

all required prediction streams are active;
timestamps are valid;
device clocks are synchronized;
prediction timing is within the configured synchronization tolerance; and
the synchronization queue is receiving all streams.



System Remains in Fallback Mode
Verify that all five edge nodes have resumed publishing current predictions.
The watchdog should return the system to normal synchronized operation once all required streams are healthy again.
